verifyNote: Written from standard vision science and visual perception teaching on UK optometry degrees, with College of Optometrists and DVLA guidance where relevant. Normal values differ between tests and sources: use the norms your department teaches.

topics.title: Visual acuity and contrast sensitivity
topics.summary: Visual acuity measures the finest detail an eye can resolve at high contrast; contrast sensitivity measures how faint a pattern can be and still be seen. Acuity is recorded in Snellen or logMAR notation. Contrast sensitivity can be reduced even when acuity is normal, for example in cataract, glaucoma and optic nerve disease.
keyPoints: A 6/6 letter subtends 5 minutes of arc overall at 6 m, with each stroke 1 minute of arc (the minimum angle of resolution, MAR, is 1′).
LogMAR = log₁₀(MAR). 6/6 = 0.00, 6/12 = 0.30, 6/60 = 1.00. Lower is better; many young adults see about −0.10.
On logMAR (ETDRS-style) charts each line is 0.1 and each letter 0.02, with five letters per line and equal spacing.
Contrast sensitivity is the reciprocal of threshold contrast. The contrast sensitivity function peaks at about 3–5 cycles per degree and cuts off at about 50–60 c/deg.
The Pelli-Robson chart uses letters of one size that fade in steps of 0.15 log units; normal adults score about 1.65 log CS or better.
Michelson contrast = (Lmax − Lmin) / (Lmax + Lmin), used for gratings; Weber contrast = (L − Lbackground) / Lbackground, used for letters.
examTraps: Writing logMAR scores as if higher is better: lower logMAR means better acuity.
Assuming normal acuity means normal vision: contrast sensitivity can be reduced first.
Forgetting to score letter by letter on a logMAR chart.

diagram.description: A graph with spatial frequency (cycles per degree, log scale, 0.5 to 60) on the x-axis and contrast sensitivity (log scale) on the y-axis. Draw an inverted-U curve peaking at about 4 c/deg and falling to the acuity cut-off at about 50 c/deg. Add a second, lower curve labelled 'cataract' showing loss mainly at mid and high frequencies.

goDeeper.heading: Converting Snellen and logMAR
goDeeper.body: MAR (in minutes of arc) = Snellen denominator ÷ numerator. 6/9 → MAR 1.5 → logMAR 0.18 (recorded 0.2 to the nearest line). 6/18 → MAR 3 → 0.48 (0.5). 6/36 → MAR 6 → 0.78 (0.8). To score a logMAR chart letter by letter: start from the logMAR of the last line read fully, then subtract 0.02 for each extra letter read on the next line.

goDeeper.heading: Why logMAR charts are better
goDeeper.body: Snellen charts have different numbers of letters per line and uneven steps, so a 'one-line' change means different amounts in different parts of the chart. LogMAR charts have the same number of letters per line, equal spacing proportional to letter size, and equal log steps, which makes them more repeatable and better for tracking change, research and children's amblyopia treatment.

goDeeper.heading: When contrast sensitivity matters
goDeeper.body: Patients with early cataract, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, optic neuritis or after refractive surgery may read 6/6 yet complain that things look washed out, especially in low light or glare. A Pelli-Robson score, or a glare test, can show the problem and supports referral or advice. Low contrast sensitivity also predicts difficulties with mobility and driving at night.

topics.title: Colour vision and colour vision deficiency
topics.summary: Colour vision starts with three cone types (S, M and L) and is then recoded in the retina and brain into opposing channels (red–green, blue–yellow, light–dark). About 8% of men and 0.5% of women have an inherited red–green deficiency. Acquired defects from eye disease are often blue–yellow and can be an early sign of a problem.
keyPoints: Trichromatic theory (Young–Helmholtz) explains the cones; opponent-process theory (Hering) explains later processing. Both are correct at different stages.
Congenital red–green deficiency is X-linked recessive: about 8% of males and 0.5% of females.
Protan defects involve L cones and deutan defects M cones; deuteranomaly is the most common type.
Tritan (S-cone) defects are rare congenitally (autosomal dominant) but common in acquired disease such as glaucoma, diabetic eye disease and cataract.

Ishihara screens for red–green defects only; tests such as HRR and City University include tritan plates; the Farnsworth D-15 grades severity; the anomaloscope is the reference test for classification.
Some jobs have colour vision standards (for example aviation, some armed forces and rail roles).
examTraps: Using Ishihara to rule out a blue–yellow defect: it doesn't test for it.
Calling colour deficiency 'colour blindness': most people with it see colours, just differently.
Forgetting that a new colour vision change in one eye is acquired and needs investigating.

diagram.description: Three overlapping bell-shaped sensitivity curves on a wavelength axis from 400 to 700 nm: S cones peaking near 420 nm, M near 530 nm and L near 560 nm. Below, draw the opponent channels: L − M (red–green), S − (L + M) (blue–yellow) and L + M (luminance).

goDeeper.heading: Types of inherited deficiency
goDeeper.body: Anomalous trichromats have all three cone types, but one has a shifted sensitivity (protanomaly, deuteranomaly, tritanomaly). Dichromats lack one cone type (protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia). Monochromats are very rare: rod monochromats (achromatopsia) have poor acuity, photophobia and nystagmus. Protans also see reds as darker than normal.

goDeeper.heading: Choosing a colour vision test
goDeeper.body: Ishihara: quick red–green screening, good sensitivity. HRR (Hardy–Rand–Rittler): screens red–green and blue–yellow and gives an idea of severity. City University and D-15: arrangement or matching tests that show the confusion axis and severity. Anomaloscope (Nagel type): mixes red and green to match yellow; the gold standard for classifying red–green defects. Test each eye separately when looking for acquired defects.

goDeeper.heading: Acquired colour defects
goDeeper.body: Köllner's rule: outer retinal (and media) disease tends to cause blue–yellow defects, while optic nerve disease tends to cause red–green defects, though there are exceptions. Optic neuritis, for example, often reduces red saturation ('red desaturation'), which can be checked by comparing how red a target looks to each eye.

cases.scenario: A 16-year-old boy wants to become an airline pilot. He fails several Ishihara plates.
cases.question: What would you do and say?
cases.modelAnswer: Confirm the result and classify it (for example with City University, HRR or D-15, and refer for an anomaloscope if needed). Explain that he has an inherited red–green deficiency that won't change. Some careers, including pilots, have specific colour vision standards and their own approved tests, so advise him to check the current requirements with the relevant regulator early before committing to a career path.

topics.title: Light and dark adaptation
topics.summary: The visual system works over a huge range of light levels by switching between cones (photopic vision) and rods (scotopic vision) and by adjusting sensitivity. Dark adaptation takes up to about 30–40 minutes and has a cone phase and a rod phase; light adaptation happens within seconds.
keyPoints: Photopic vision (cones): good acuity and colour. Scotopic vision (rods): very sensitive, no colour, poor acuity. Mesopic: both working.
The dark adaptation curve has two branches: cones plateau after about 5–10 minutes, then the rod–cone break, then rods continue for about 30–40 minutes.
Rods are slower to recover because rhodopsin takes longer to regenerate.
Purkinje shift: peak sensitivity moves from about 555 nm (photopic) to about 507 nm (scotopic), so blues look brighter at dusk and reds darker.
Pupil size, photopigment bleaching and neural changes all contribute to adaptation.
Poor night vision can be an early sign of retinitis pigmentosa or vitamin A deficiency; older eyes also adapt more slowly.
examTraps: Saying the fovea is the most sensitive area in dim light: it has no rods, so looking slightly off to the side helps.
Forgetting that pupil changes account for only a small part of adaptation.
Mixing up the order of the curve: cones first, rods later.

diagram.description: A graph of threshold (log luminance, y-axis, decreasing upwards meaning more sensitive) against time in the dark (minutes, x-axis, 0–40). Draw a fast first branch levelling at about 7 minutes (cones), a kink (rod–cone break) and a slower second branch continuing to fall until about 30–40 minutes (rods).

goDeeper.heading: Why rods take longer
goDeeper.body: Bright light bleaches a large proportion of photopigment. Cone pigment regenerates quickly, so cone sensitivity recovers within minutes. Rhodopsin regeneration needs the RPE to recycle retinal and is much slower, so full rod sensitivity takes up to about 40 minutes. Testing with a deep red light lets you see the cone branch alone because rods are insensitive to long wavelengths.

goDeeper.heading: Clinical night vision problems
goDeeper.body: Night blindness (nyctalopia) occurs in retinitis pigmentosa (rods are affected first), vitamin A deficiency (needed for rhodopsin), some forms of congenital stationary night blindness, and after extensive laser treatment of the retina. Older people have smaller pupils, yellower lenses and slower adaptation, so night driving is harder.

goDeeper.heading: The Purkinje shift in practice
goDeeper.body: At dusk, red flowers look dark and blue ones relatively bright because rods are most sensitive to blue-green light. Instrument panels and red light in darkrooms or observatories use long wavelengths so the rods stay dark adapted.

flashcards.front: How long does full dark adaptation take?

flashcards.back: The kink in the dark adaptation curve where rods become more sensitive than cones.

topics.title: Visual fields
topics.summary: The visual field is everything an eye sees while looking straight ahead. It's measured by finding the dimmest or smallest target seen at each place (static perimetry) or by moving a target in from the edge (kinetic perimetry). Field tests are essential in glaucoma, neurological disease and for the DVLA driving standard.
keyPoints: Approximate normal extent of one eye: about 60° up, 60° nasal, 70–75° down and 90–100° temporal. Both eyes together cover about 180° horizontally.
Sensitivity is highest at fixation and falls towards the edge: the 'hill of vision'.
The physiological blind spot is about 15° temporal and slightly below the horizontal, about 5° wide and 7° tall.
Static automated perimetry (for example Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2) tests set points; kinetic perimetry (for example Goldmann) maps isopters.
Reliability indices: fixation losses, false positives and false negatives.
DVLA Group 1 (car) standard: a horizontal field of at least 120° with no significant defect within 20° of fixation (tested binocularly with an Esterman programme).
examTraps: Interpreting a field with poor reliability without retesting.
Confusing an absolute scotoma (nothing seen) with a relative one (only brighter targets seen).
Forgetting the learning effect: first-time field tests are often worse than later ones.

diagram.description: A 3D 'island' shaped hill of vision with its peak at fixation, sloping down towards the edges, with a deep narrow pit (the blind spot) about 15° temporal. Beside it, a flat plot of one eye's field with the blind spot marked and approximate extents (60° up, 60° nasal, 75° down, 95° temporal).

goDeeper.heading: Static and kinetic perimetry
goDeeper.body: Static: the target stays still and its brightness changes until a threshold is found at each tested point. It's sensitive to shallow, early loss and is standard in glaucoma. Kinetic: a target of fixed size and brightness moves in from the edge; the boundary where it's first seen is an isopter. Kinetic testing is good for mapping the whole field and for patients who can't do long automated tests.

goDeeper.heading: Reading a field printout
goDeeper.body: Check the patient's details, test and reliability first. Then look at the grey scale for the overall picture, the total and pattern deviation plots for where loss is, and the global indices (mean deviation and pattern standard deviation, or equivalents). Glaucoma tends to cause arcuate, nasal step or paracentral defects that respect the horizontal midline; neurological defects respect the vertical midline.

goDeeper.heading: Driving and fields
goDeeper.body: If a patient's fields may not meet the DVLA standard, the patient has a legal duty to tell the DVLA. The optometrist should explain this clearly and record the advice. The DVLA arranges its own Esterman binocular test with an approved provider. The College of Optometrists has guidance on what to do if a patient won't stop driving.

flashcards.back: About 15° temporal to fixation, just below the horizontal.

flashcards.front: Three reliability indices on automated fields

At least 120° horizontally, no significant defect within 20° of fixation (binocular Esterman).

cases.modelAnswer: Explain that his fields may not meet the DVLA standard, that he has a legal duty to tell the DVLA and should not drive until they decide, and record this advice clearly. topics.title: Depth perception and stereopsis
topics.summary: We judge depth from many monocular cues, such as size, overlap and motion, and from binocular disparity, the small difference between the two eyes' images. Stereopsis is the fine depth sense that disparity gives. It needs two well-aligned eyes with good, similar vision, so it is reduced in amblyopia and strabismus.
keyPoints: Monocular cues: relative size, overlap (interposition), linear perspective, texture gradient, shading, aerial perspective and motion parallax.
Binocular disparity: objects nearer or further than the fixation point fall on non-corresponding retinal points.
The horopter is the set of points seen singly with no disparity; Panum's fusional area is the small zone around it that can still be fused.
Normal stereoacuity is about 60 seconds of arc or better on most clinical tests (often 40″ or less).
Clinical tests: TNO and Randot (random-dot, need glasses), Frisby (real depth, no glasses) and Lang (for young children).
Reduced stereoacuity is a useful sign of amblyopia or strabismus, especially in children.
examTraps: Thinking people with one eye have no depth perception: they use monocular cues.
Forgetting that monocular cues can be used to 'cheat' some contour-based stereo tests.
Mixing up the horopter (zero disparity) with Panum's area (the fusible range around it).

diagram.description: Top view of two eyes fixating a point F. Draw the curved horopter through F, a shaded Panum's fusional area around it, an object nearer than F (crossed disparity) and one further away (uncrossed disparity), with lines showing where each falls on the two retinas.

goDeeper.heading: Random-dot tests
goDeeper.body: Random-dot stereograms (TNO, Randot preschool) hide the shape in a pattern of dots that looks the same to each eye on its own. The shape only appears when the two images are fused with disparity, so they can't be passed with monocular cues. That makes them good screening tests for binocular problems.

goDeeper.heading: Crossed and uncrossed disparity
goDeeper.body: Objects nearer than fixation give crossed disparity (images fall outwards on each retina); objects further away give uncrossed disparity. Small disparities are seen as depth; larger ones beyond Panum's area cause double vision (physiological diplopia), which we usually ignore.

goDeeper.heading: Stereopsis and everyday life
goDeeper.body: Stereopsis matters most for fine near tasks: threading a needle, pouring liquid, catching and some jobs (for example surgery). Many people with poor stereopsis manage well using monocular cues. Sudden loss of stereo or new double vision, however, suggests a new binocular problem.

topics.title: Motion, form and visual illusions
topics.summary: After the retina, visual information splits into pathways specialised for different jobs. The magnocellular pathway is fast and sensitive to motion and flicker; the parvocellular pathway handles fine detail and red–green colour. Cortical areas then build up shapes, objects and motion. Visual illusions reveal the rules the system uses.
keyPoints: Ganglion cells have centre–surround receptive fields (ON-centre or OFF-centre), which makes them respond best to edges and contrast.
Magnocellular pathway: large cells, fast, high temporal resolution, motion, low contrast. Parvocellular: small cells, fine detail, red–green colour.
Area V5 (MT) is specialised for motion; damage can cause akinetopsia (motion blindness).
The ventral ('what') stream recognises objects and faces; the dorsal ('where/how') stream guides action and spatial awareness.
Lateral inhibition explains Mach bands and the Hermann grid illusion.
Gestalt principles (proximity, similarity, continuity, closure) describe how features are grouped into objects.
examTraps: Saying the parvocellular pathway handles motion: it's mainly magnocellular.
Thinking illusions are 'mistakes': they show the normal rules the visual system uses.
Mixing up the ventral and dorsal streams.

diagram.description: Two circular receptive fields: ON-centre (bright centre +, dark surround −) and OFF-centre (the reverse). Below, a Hermann grid (black squares separated by white lines) showing faint grey spots at the intersections, with an explanation arrow to lateral inhibition.

goDeeper.heading: Lateral inhibition
goDeeper.body: Neighbouring cells inhibit each other. A cell looking at a white line between two black squares has dark either side, so little inhibition. At an intersection there is white on four sides, more inhibition, so the intersection looks greyer. The same mechanism sharpens edges (Mach bands), which helps us see boundaries clearly.

goDeeper.heading: Two streams beyond V1
goDeeper.body: The ventral stream runs to the temporal lobe and handles object recognition, colour and faces; damage can cause visual agnosia or prosopagnosia (face blindness). The dorsal stream runs to the parietal lobe and handles motion, location and guiding movements; damage can cause problems reaching for objects or with spatial awareness, such as visual neglect.

goDeeper.heading: Flicker and temporal vision
goDeeper.body: The critical flicker fusion frequency is the rate at which a flickering light looks steady, roughly 50–60 Hz at high brightness and lower in dim light. It is reduced in some optic nerve diseases. Faster temporal processing in the periphery is why you may notice flicker from the corner of your eye that disappears when you look straight at it.

'What': object, colour and face recognition (temporal lobe).

flashcards.front: Mechanism behind the Hermann grid illusion

topics.title: Psychophysics: thresholds and how they are measured
topics.summary: Psychophysics links physical stimuli to what people perceive. Almost every clinical test, from acuity to visual fields, finds a threshold: the weakest stimulus that can be detected or the smallest difference that can be told apart. How the threshold is measured affects how accurate, quick and biased the result is.
keyPoints: Absolute threshold: the weakest stimulus detected. Difference threshold (just noticeable difference): the smallest detectable change.
The psychometric function plots probability of seeing against stimulus strength; threshold is usually set at 50% (or 75% in two-alternative forced choice).
Methods: limits (ascending/descending), adjustment (patient controls the stimulus), constant stimuli (random set levels), and adaptive staircases.
Forced-choice methods (for example 'which interval had the target?') reduce the effect of the patient's response bias.
Weber's law: the just noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the starting intensity (ΔI / I = constant).
Signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d′) from the criterion a person uses to say 'yes'.
examTraps: Saying the method of constant stimuli is quick: it's accurate but slow.
Forgetting that 'yes/no' tasks are affected by how cautious the patient is.
Treating threshold as a fixed line: perception is probabilistic.

diagram.description: An S-shaped curve of percentage correct (y-axis, 0–100%) against stimulus intensity (x-axis). Mark the 50% point for a yes/no task. Add a second curve for a two-alternative forced-choice task starting at 50% (guessing) and rising to 100%, with threshold marked at 75%.

goDeeper.heading: Clinical methods in disguise
goDeeper.body: Visual acuity charts use a method of limits (smaller and smaller letters). Automated perimeters use staircases with 4 dB and then 2 dB steps (or faster strategies such as SITA) to find threshold at each point. Preferential looking in babies is a forced-choice method: the tester judges which side the baby looks towards.

goDeeper.heading: Signal detection theory
goDeeper.body: Every response falls into hits, misses, false alarms or correct rejections. Sensitivity (d′) reflects how well the stimulus can be distinguished from noise; the criterion reflects willingness to say 'seen'. A cautious patient has few false alarms but more misses; an eager one the opposite. False-positive catch trials in perimetry estimate this bias.

goDeeper.heading: Weber's law
goDeeper.body: If you can just tell 100 from 102 units (2%), you'll need about 200 vs 204 at double the level. Weber fractions are roughly constant across a wide middle range of intensities but break down at very low and very high levels. Fechner built on this to suggest perceived magnitude grows with the logarithm of intensity, one reason clinical scales such as decibels and logMAR are logarithmic.
